obs-sentry-langfuse.md:
## Why it exists
Two different questions come up in production. **Is the app broken or slow?** and **Is the AI behaving well, and what does it cost?** Sentry answers the first and Langfuse the second. Used together they give the whole picture.

{{dg:0}}

## Sentry: errors and performance
Sentry groups exceptions into **issues**, captures stack traces and breadcrumbs, and ties them to a **release** and an **environment** so you know which deploy broke what. **Tracing** shows slow requests and database calls.
```python
import os, sentry_sdk

sentry_sdk.init(
    dsn=os.environ['SENTRY_DSN'],
    environment=os.getenv('ENV', 'dev'),
    release=os.getenv('GIT_SHA'),          # tie errors to a deploy
    traces_sample_rate=0.1,                # sample 10 percent of requests
    send_default_pii=False,
)
# Web frameworks such as FastAPI and Flask are detected automatically.
```
```ts
import * as Sentry from '@sentry/node'

Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN,
  environment: process.env.NODE_ENV,
  release: process.env.GIT_SHA,
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
})
```
For Next.js use the `@sentry/nextjs` package. Its setup wizard (`npx @sentry/wizard@latest -i nextjs`) creates the configuration files. Upload source maps in CI so stack traces show your original code.

## Langfuse: tracing LLM apps
Langfuse records each LLM request as a **trace** of nested **observations** (spans, generations, retrievals, tool calls) with inputs, outputs, latency, tokens and cost. It also stores **prompts**, **datasets**, **scores** and experiments.
```python
from langfuse import observe, get_client
from langfuse.openai import openai       # drop-in wrapper that logs model, tokens and cost

client = openai.AsyncOpenAI()

@observe()                                # becomes a span in the trace
async def retrieve(question: str) -> list[str]:
    return await vector_search(question, k=5)

@observe()                                # parent span: retrieval and the model call nest under it
async def answer(question: str) -> str:
    docs = await retrieve(question)
    res = await client.chat.completions.create(
        model='gpt-4o-mini',              # placeholder: use your own provider and model
        messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': f'{docs}\n\nQ: {question}'}],
    )
    return res.choices[0].message.content

get_client().flush()                      # in scripts and serverless, flush before exit
```
Set `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`, `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY` and `LANGFUSE_BASE_URL`. For other providers, wrap the call in a generation observation and record the model and usage. Attach user, session and tags with the SDK's trace-attribute helpers. The exact helper names changed between SDK major versions, so confirm them in the current docs.

## Using them together
| Question | Tool | What you see |
|---|---|---|
| Why did the endpoint return 500? | Sentry | Stack trace, release, affected users |
| Why is it slow? | Both | Sentry trace shows the slow span; Langfuse shows the LLM step |
| Why was the answer wrong? | Langfuse | Retrieved chunks, prompt version, model output |
| What does this feature cost? | Langfuse | Tokens and cost per user or per trace |
| Did the last prompt change hurt quality? | Langfuse | Experiment scores against a dataset |

Share one request or trace id: add the Langfuse trace id as a Sentry tag, and the Sentry event id into Langfuse metadata, so you can jump between them.

## In real products
- Alert in Sentry on new issues and error-rate spikes. Review Langfuse dashboards for cost per user and low-scoring traces.
- Add user feedback (thumbs) as Langfuse scores, then promote bad traces into your eval dataset.
- Roll out prompt changes from Langfuse prompt management using labels (staging, production) and compare versions.

> [!security] Both tools receive your data. Scrub PII and secrets before they leave the app, set sampling rates, and decide retention. Do not log raw prompts that contain personal data unless you must.
> [!pitfall] Sampling away the traces you need. Keep full traces for errors and low-scoring runs, and sample the high-volume happy path.
> [!cost] Traces cost storage and money at scale. Review volume monthly and set limits.
q: Which tool would you open first for a 500 error, and which for a wrong answer?
Sentry for the 500 error and its stack trace; Langfuse for a wrong answer, to inspect retrieved context, prompt and output.
Why set a release value in Sentry?
It ties each error to a deploy, so you can see which version introduced a regression.

obs-sre-slos.md:
## Why it exists
Developers want to ship features, operators want stability, and without numbers every outage becomes an argument. **Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)** started at Google as a way to run production with software engineering methods. Its central idea: **100% reliability is the wrong target**. It is impossibly expensive, users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% because their own network is less reliable, and a system that never changes cannot improve.

So you pick a target below 100%, measure against it, and treat the gap as a **budget** you are allowed to spend on releases, experiments and risk.

{{dg:0}}

Mental model: **SLI** is a thermometer, **SLO** is the temperature you promise to stay under, **SLA** is the contract with penalties, and the **error budget** is how much failure the SLO allows.

## How it works
- **SLI (service level indicator).** A ratio: good events divided by valid events, as a percentage. Availability: successful requests / all requests. Latency: requests faster than 300 ms / all requests. Freshness: data updated within 5 minutes / all checks. Measure from the user's side where you can (load balancer, client, synthetic probe), not only inside the process.
- **SLO (service level objective).** A target for an SLI over a window, for example "99.9% of checkout requests succeed over a rolling 30 days". Fewer, user-centered SLOs beat dozens of technical ones.
- **SLA (service level agreement).** A legal or commercial promise with consequences. Keep your SLO stricter than your SLA so you notice trouble before you owe refunds.
- **Error budget.** `1 - SLO` expressed as time or requests. At 99.9% over 30 days you may fail 0.1%: about 43.2 minutes of full outage, or 1 in 1,000 requests.
- **Error budget policy.** A written agreement on what happens when the budget runs low: freeze risky launches, prioritize reliability work, escalate. Without a policy the number is decoration.
- **Burn rate.** How fast the budget is being consumed relative to plan. Burn rate 1 uses exactly the whole budget by the end of the window; 14.4 would burn 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour.
- **Golden signals / RED / USE.** Latency, traffic, errors, saturation (Google); Rate, Errors, Duration for services (RED); Utilization, Saturation, Errors for resources (USE). They tell you what to instrument first.
- **Percentiles, not averages.** An average of 200 ms can hide a p99 of 8 seconds. SLOs on latency should use thresholds or percentiles from histograms.

| SLO | Allowed downtime per 30 days | Per year |
|---|---|---|
| 99% | 7.2 hours | 3.65 days |
| 99.9% | 43.2 minutes | 8.76 hours |
| 99.95% | 21.6 minutes | 4.38 hours |
| 99.99% | 4.32 minutes | 52.6 minutes |

{{dg:1}}

## Worked example
Budget arithmetic and a request-based SLI in Python:

```python
def budget_minutes(slo: float, days: int = 30) -> float:
    return (1 - slo) * days * 24 * 60

for slo in (0.99, 0.999, 0.9995, 0.9999):
    print(f"{slo:.2%} -> {budget_minutes(slo):.2f} min per 30 days")

def sli(good: int, valid: int) -> float:
    return good / valid if valid else 1.0

# 1,000,000 requests this window, 1,400 failed
used = (1 - sli(998_600, 1_000_000)) / (1 - 0.999)
print(f"budget consumed: {used:.0%}")   # 140% -> over budget, apply the policy
```

The same idea in Prometheus: recording rules for the SLI and a multi-window burn-rate alert for a 99.9% availability SLO (budget 0.001).

```yaml
groups:
  - name: checkout-slo
    rules:
      - record: sli:availability:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",code!~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
      - record: sli:availability:ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",code!~"5.."}[1h]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[1h]))
      # Fast burn: 14.4x over 1h AND 5m confirms it is still happening -> page
      - alert: CheckoutFastBurn
        expr: |
          (1 - sli:availability:ratio_rate1h) > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          (1 - sli:availability:ratio_rate5m) > (14.4 * 0.001)
        for: 2m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout is burning its 30-day error budget 14x too fast"
```

A latency SLI from a histogram: share of requests under 300 ms.

```promql
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout",le="0.3"}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="checkout"}[5m]))
```

## In real products
- **Alerting on burn rate** (from the Google SRE Workbook) replaces threshold alerts like "5xx above 1%". A common set: page at 14.4x over 1 hour (2% of budget gone), page at 6x over 6 hours (5%), ticket at 1x over 3 days (10%). Each pairs a long window with a short one to avoid noisy or stale alerts.
- **Tooling.** Datadog SLOs, Grafana SLO, Google Cloud Service Monitoring, Nobl9, Sloth and the OpenSLO spec all generate this math. CloudWatch and Azure Monitor can compute the same ratios from metrics.
- **LLM applications.** Add AI-specific SLIs next to availability: p95 time to first token, share of responses passing an automated eval, cost per request, and tool-call error rate. Langfuse and Sentry (see the observability lesson) supply the events.
- **Process.** Weekly SLO review, incident postmortems feed back into SLOs, and on-call load is capped. Eliminating **toil** (manual, repetitive, automatable work) is an explicit SRE goal, often held under 50% of engineers' time.
- **Chaos engineering and game days** test whether alerts, runbooks and failover work before a real incident does.

## Trade-offs
| Choice | Option A | Option B | Guidance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Window | Rolling 28 or 30 days | Calendar month | Rolling is smoother; calendar matches billing and reports |
| Counting | Request-based (good/valid) | Time-based (good minutes) | Request-based fits traffic that varies; time-based fits probes and low traffic |
| Target | 99.9% | 99.99% | Each extra nine costs far more; match it to what users actually notice |
| Scope | One SLO per user journey | One SLO per microservice | Start from journeys; services inherit from them |

> [!pitfall] Choosing SLIs because they are easy: CPU, memory or "server up". Users feel failed checkouts and slow pages, not CPU.
> [!pitfall] SLO equals SLA. Then the first breach is already a contractual penalty. Keep an internal margin.
> [!pitfall] Averages. Use histograms and percentiles; one slow dependency can wreck p99 while the mean looks fine.
> [!pitfall] Counting 4xx caused by bad client input as errors, or hiding real failures behind a 200 with an error body. Define "good" carefully.
> [!tip] Start with one or two SLOs on your most important journey, run them for a month, then tighten. Reality beats guessing.
> [!tip] Too many pages is the usual failure. Every page must be urgent, actionable and need a human; everything else becomes a ticket.
> [!prod] When the budget is exhausted, the policy decides: freeze feature releases, fix top causes, or renegotiate the SLO if it is unrealistic. Document the decision in the postmortem.
q: What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA?

The SLI is the measurement (good events divided by valid events), the SLO is the internal target for it over a window, and the SLA is the external contract with consequences. The SLO should be stricter than the SLA.
Compute the error budget for a 99.95% SLO over 30 days.
0.05% of 43,200 minutes is 21.6 minutes of full outage, or 1 failed request in 2,000.
Why alert on burn rate instead of a fixed error percentage?

Burn rate ties the alert to how fast the budget is being consumed, so a short severe incident pages immediately while a slow leak becomes a ticket. Fixed thresholds miss slow burns or page on harmless blips.
Why is 100% a bad reliability target?
It is unattainable and extremely expensive, users cannot perceive the difference beyond their own network reliability, and it forbids any change. A budget below 100% pays for shipping.
Name three SLIs for an LLM-powered feature.
Availability of the endpoint, p95 time to first token, and the share of responses passing an automated quality eval. Cost per request and tool-call error rate are also common.
